segments.text: In the monsoon, the rivers of the Peshawar Valley rise and fall under thick cloud. Optical satellites often see only the cloud. Radar sees through it. This is SARtale: nine passes of the NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite, from July to October 2026, and one question. What changed, when did it change, and how far can we trust the answer?

NISAR sends microwave pulses down and measures what comes back. Calm water acts like a mirror and sends the energy away, so it looks dark. Rough ground and buildings scatter energy back, so they look bright. We express gamma-zero backscatter in decibels: ten times its base-ten logarithm. A rise of ten decibels means ten times the power. NISAR also measures two polarizations. HH sends horizontal and receives horizontal. HV sends horizontal and receives vertical. They respond differently, and that will matter.

Pick one place: the south-east shore of Tarbela Reservoir. Each dot is one pass. In July, HH sits around minus seven decibels. By the nineteenth of August, it has fallen to minus sixteen point six. The obvious idea is to compare each date with the median of the other eligible dates. Here, that fails. Most of the season is dark, so dark becomes normal, and the big August change barely scores.

So we ask a better question. Suppose there was one moment of change. Split the season in two, and take the mean before and the mean after. The gap between them is the step. Now slide that split across the season, keeping at least two dates on each side. A big gap means little if the points are noisy, so we divide by how much they scatter around their own means, adjusted for how many dates sit on each side. That gives a stability score. For this shore, the best split falls between the twenty-sixth of July and the nineteenth of August: a step of about minus eight decibels in HH, minus five in HV, with a stability near six.

A pixel is flagged only when three things hold. HH and HV must move the same way. Their average absolute step must be at least three decibels. And their combined stability must be at least three. The map groups pixels into cells coloured by the most common flagged step date and direction.

Is that just noise? Choosing the best of several splits inflates the scores, so we test it. Shuffle the dates at each pixel and run everything again. The real order flags 1.39 percent of the map. The shuffled version flags 0.25 percent. Shuffling the whole scene together, two hundred times, never reached the real figure. Stable ground stayed quiet too: nothing flagged at Peshawar city or in the main Tarbela pool at the sites we chart. One caution: the rule was set with the known sites in view, so this was not a blind test.

Honest work also shows what it cannot see. On the second of July, HV jumped about fourteen decibels over the west of the map, while HH barely moved. That is likely radio interference, so the date is left out of the change analysis. The highest listed flow at Nowshera, seventy-eight thousand five hundred cusecs, came on the twenty-third of July, between two passes. And NISAR has a permanent data gap from the twenty-seventh of July to the tenth of August.
Here is the app. It opens on the finding, with the real radar image behind it. Start the story, and ten guided steps move the map to each place.
Leave the story at any time and explore freely. Step through the dates, switch between HH and HV, and compare any two passes with a before and after slider.
Turn on Change to see the step map. Each colour is a date. Light tints went brighter, and deep shades went darker. The key sits beside the map.
Site Stories puts the real curve first. Every card separates what was observed from the hypothesis, what would test it, and its limits.
What NISAR Missed shows every pass and the gap. And How We Know sets out the data, the method, the checks and the limits.

A step is not a cause. Plain ground flags too, and we do not yet know why. The data is provisional, and this is not a warning service. But in one season of open NASA data, we can show what radar saw, when it changed, and how much to trust it. This is SARtale, by team SARcastic Scientists.
